questions.q: In 'UPDATE dbo.LessonDemo SET ListPrice = ListPrice * 0.90 WHERE Color = 'Red' AND ListPrice > 1000;', which rows get the discount?
options: Every row that is Red, regardless of price
Every row in the table
Only rows that are both Red AND priced over 1000
Every row priced over 1000, regardless of color
questions.explain: Combining conditions with AND narrows the UPDATE to only rows that satisfy both conditions at once.

questions.q: In the pattern 'UPDATE d SET d.ListPrice = p.ListPrice FROM dbo.LessonDemo AS d JOIN Production.Product AS p ON d.ProductName = p.Name;', what comes right after the UPDATE keyword?
options: The column being set
The literal table name dbo.LessonDemo
The table alias (d), not the literal table name
The FROM keyword
questions.explain: The standard joined-UPDATE shape names the alias right after UPDATE; the real table and its alias are defined later in FROM.

questions.q: What happens to a row in dbo.LessonDemo that has no matching row in Production.Product under an inner JOIN update?
options: It causes the whole UPDATE statement to fail
It is deleted automatically
It is updated with NULL values
It is left untouched -- only rows with a match in the join are updated
questions.explain: An inner join only updates rows that find a matching partner row, exactly like it would exclude unmatched rows from a SELECT.

questions.q: In a joined UPDATE, what is the difference between the ON clause and an additional WHERE clause?
options: ON and WHERE do exactly the same thing and can be used interchangeably
WHERE decides which rows match; ON filters them afterward
ON can only be used with SELECT, never with UPDATE
ON decides which rows match in the join; WHERE further filters the matched pairs
questions.explain: ON controls how the two tables are paired up; WHERE then restricts which of those already-matched pairs get updated.

questions.q: Why does the SET clause in a joined UPDATE reference the alias (e.g. d.ListPrice) rather than just the column name?
options: Because ListPrice only exists on the aliased table
Because SET requires every column to be prefixed with d. by syntax rule
Aliases are only needed when WHERE is omitted
Because the statement involves two tables, and the alias makes clear which table's column is being set or read
questions.explain: With two tables in play (d and p), prefixing columns with their alias avoids ambiguity about which table's column is meant.
